title: With AI platform, patients could chat with medical devices to improve health
source_used: Penn Engineering news and healthcare-in-europe.com (Washington Post page not opened, HTTP 000)
key_facts: Penn researchers built an AI platform letting patients message their medical devices from a phone app.
Proof-of-concept study with 13 adults undergoing EEG brain monitoring in Penn's Epilepsy Monitoring Unit.
Researchers analysed 1,307 messages; patients asked about brain activity, reported symptoms and corrected seizure detections.
Patient feedback substantially improved the system's ability to identify seizures.
Findings published in Nature Medicine; senior author Brian Litt, professor of neurology, neurosurgery and bioengineering.
Team plans work on tuning deep brain stimulation for Parkinson's disease; supported by a $5.6 million NIH Pioneer Award.
Ongoing research will test whether it reduces seizure frequency, ER visits and costs.
quote_evidence: Participants in a proof-of-concept study undergoing monitoring for seizures could ask questions about their brain activity, receive personalized alerts, report symptoms and behaviors, and help train the system to better recognize seizure-related patterns.
researchers enrolled 13 adults undergoing continuous brain monitoring using electroencephalogram (EEG)
why_it_matters_hint: Moves medical devices from passive recorders toward two-way partners, but only tested on 13 hospital patients so far.
notes: Washington Post page unreachable; used the Penn release (the researchers' own account). Whether outcomes improve is not yet shown.
